title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarks, Runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel-scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, operational runbooks, known issues, and team wiki pointers. It is the canonical reference for engineers working on the inference serving runtime and for oncall SREs responding to performance incidents.

Goals
- Provide a single, searchable reference that links architecture, schedulers, and operational procedures.
- Standardize profiling and benchmarking methods so results are comparable across models, hardware, and releases.
- Document deterministic runbooks for common incidents (latency regressions, OOMs, soft-failures).

Scope and audience
- Audience: Serving runtime engineers, infra/SRE, performance/benchmarking team, and reliability engineers.
- Scope: GPU-backed inference runtime (hosted and dedicated modes). Does not cover private deployment networking or tenant billing flows in detail; see related pages.

1) Architecture overview

Summary
The serving runtime is composed of: request ingress, front-tier routing, model runtime (per-model executor), kernel selection and scheduler, KV/prefix cache, batching layer, and egress/telemetry. The runtime is GPU-first; CPU is used for request orchestration, tokenization, and light-weight preprocessing.

Key components
- Ingress & routing: route-service (policy: latency/cost/region/fallback).
- Model executor: per-model process that owns model weights and KV cache. Supports quantized and full-precision variants.
- Scheduler & kernel selector: chooses kernel implementations and schedules GPU work to maximize throughput while meeting latency SLOs.
- Batcher: continuous batching layer that groups compatible requests within latency windows.
- Cache: prefix and KV cache to short-circuit repeated prefixes and reduce token compute.
- Telemetry: per-token tracing, token-level cost breakdowns, and model-level perf counters.

Architecture diagram (textual)
Ingress -> Routing -> Batcher -> Scheduler (+ Kernel selector) -> Model Executor (CUDA kernels, KV cache) -> Egress + Telemetry

SLOs (service-level)
- Latency p95 target: 200 ms for single-token step on g4dn-class machines (adjust by machine class).
- Tail latency (p99): < 500 ms under nominal load.
- Throughput SLO: 80% of provisioned GPU throughput for Dedicated clusters (1-minute window).
- Error rate: <= 0.1% 5xx over 5m.

Ownership
- Runtime architecture and kernel scheduler: serving-runtime team.
- Batcher and KV cache: serving-runtime + eng-platform.
- Telemetry and dashboards: eng-platform.

2) Kernel scheduling design

Design goals
- Maximize GPU utilization without violating latency SLOs.
- Prefer low-latency kernels for small batch sizes and fuse ops for long sequences.
- Support graceful preemption and work-stealing for mixed-priority workloads.
- Be quantization-aware: some kernels are available only for int8/4 implementations.

Scheduling primitives
- Work units: per-request-token-chunk. A work unit encodes (model-version, seq_len, priority, quantization_profile).
- Queues: multiple priority queues (real-time, interactive, batch). Each GPU worker polls queues in priority order with fairness windowing.
- Scheduler policy config: configurable per-cluster via YAML: 

  scheduler_policy: 
    priority_windows_ms: [5, 20, 100]
    max_batch_size: 64
    latency_headroom_ms: 30
    preemption_enabled: true
    gpu_occupancy_target: 0.7

Kernel selection rules (summary)
1. If seq_len <= 64 and batch_size <= 8 -> choose low-latency fused-kernel (K1).
2. If quantized (int8/4) and kernel available -> choose quantized-kernel (Kq) with fallback to K1 for correctness checks.
3. For seq_len > 512 -> choose memory-optimized kernel (Km) with tiled attention.
4. If GPU occupancy < target and small kernels pending -> coalesce compatible tasks up to max_batch_size.

Preemption and fairness
- Preemption is cooperative: long-running kernel marks preemption points at attention/ffn boundaries. Preemption_enabled=true allows the scheduler to interrupt and reschedule smaller high-priority work.
- Fairness is enforced by a token-credit system: each tenant has credits decaying over time; exceeding credits lowers scheduling priority. Credits reset on low utilization windows.

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

Purpose
Provide a reproducible procedure to identify CPU/GPU hotspots, kernel inefficiencies, memory pressure, and scheduler contention that cause latency regressions or throughput drops.

Tools (approved)
- NVIDIA Nsight Systems (nsys) for end-to-end GPU+CPU traces.
- torch.profiler / PyTorch autograd profiler for operator-level visibility.
- nvprof (deprecated for some GPUs) available for legacy clusters.
- nvidia-smi and DCGM for health and utilization.
- perf, eBPF-based tools (bcc/tracee) for kernel-level CPU profiling.
- internal micro-bench harness: tools/bench_runner.py and perf-collector service.

Baseline profiling steps
1. Reproduce the issue in a dedicated perf environment that mirrors production (same machine class, driver, CUDA). Use a recorded request trace when possible.
2. Run the benchmark workload with tracing flags: 

   # capture 60s trace including warmup and steady-state
   nsys profile --output runtime_trace --trace=cuda,osrt --capture-range cstart=5s,cstop=65s --sample=cpu -- python tools/bench_runner.py --scenario recorded_trace.json --duration 70

3. Collect metrics: GPU utilization, memory utilization, PCIe throughput, CPU runqueue stats, scheduler queue lengths.
4. Open trace in Nsight GUI or use nsys stats to find long kernels (> 5 ms), frequent kernel launches, and long host-to-device memcpy.
5. Correlate with torch.profiler output to map kernels to high-level operators.
6. Identify sources: suboptimal kernel variant, serialization at host, KV cache miss storm, small-batch overhead.
7. If kernel choice is suboptimal, reproduce micro-bench per-kernel: tools/kernel_bench.py --kernel K1 --seq_len 128 --batch 4 --repeat 100
8. Propose mitigation: tweak scheduler_policy, bump occupancy target, enable coalescing, or ship a kernel patch.

Required artifacts for a profiling run (attach to ticket)
- nsys trace file (.qdrep), torch.profiler output (.json), bench_runner config, sample inputs, machine metadata (driver/CUDA/OS).

Interpreting common signals
- High kernel launch overhead + low avg GPU occupancy: indicates many tiny kernels. Consider kernel fusion or batching.
- High memcpy H2D latency: check tokenizer pre-processing and batching boundary placement.
- Growing host CPU runqueue and stalled kernels: likely CPU-side scheduling bottleneck (increase orchestration threads or move prepare work to GPU).

4) Benchmarking suite

Goals
- Standardize throughput/latency comparisons across models, quantization profiles, and machine classes.
- Maintain a historical benchmark log for every release.

Benchmark harness components
- tools/bench_runner.py: orchestrates workload (single-token step, long-context generation, chat-turns).
- scenarios/: JSON scenarios (short-prefill, long-prefill, streaming).
- dataset/: small set of representative prompts (open benchmarks + internal user traces with PII removed).
- results DB: perf-collector stores run results with tags (commit, model, machine, quant_profile).

Standard metrics recorded
- p50/p95/p99 latency per token-step (ms).
- tokens/sec throughput for steady-state generation.
- GPU utilization and percent time stalled on memcpy.
- CPU runqueue length and avg host latency.
- Memory high-water mark and OOM events.

Example benchmark command

  python tools/bench_runner.py --scenario scenarios/short-prefill.json --model redwood-small-v1 --machine_type p4d --quant_profile int8 --duration 300 --out results/redwood-small-v1-p4d-int8-2026-03-04.json

Result schema (stored separately): {commit, model, machine_type, quant_profile, p50, p95, p99, tokens_per_sec, gpu_util, memory_mb, notes} 
(Results are ingested into perf-collector; see perf dashboard link in related pages.)

Benchmark acceptance criteria for releases
1. Regression guard: p95 latency must not increase > 5% relative to baseline commit for primary workloads.
2. Throughput must not drop > 3% for dedicated capacity benchmark.
3. New kernels or quantization changes require micro-bench parity within 2% for representative sequence lengths.

5) Release notes (serving runtime releases)

Guidelines
- Every release affecting runtime must include perf impact summary, affected models, known regressions, and instructions to opt-out/rollback.
- Include perf comparison to previous stable release (automated by perf-collector).

Example recent changes (summary)
- 2026-12-01: Kernel Kq (int8) enabled by default for redwood-small-v1. Expected net token-cost reduction: 22%. Benchmarks: p95 latency +3% on p4d; rollout gated by canary policy.
- 2026-11-10: Scheduler fairness credits tuned to reduce noisy-tenant impact; reduced median latency for interactive tier by 12%.

Rollback instructions
1. Toggle kernel feature flag in cluster config: feature.kernel.Kq.enabled=false
2. Restart model-executor with zero-downtime rolling restart (see runbook below).
3. Revert scheduler policy in cluster config and reload (CLI: infractl scheduler apply --file scheduler.yaml)

6) Runtime runbooks (incident playbooks)

Runbook A: Latency spike (p95/p99 spike)
1. Check dashboards: latency by model, p95/p99, and cluster-level GPU utilization.
2. Confirm whether the spike is global or single-tenant. Filter by tenant_id.
3. If global and GPU_util is low -> suspect scheduling or kernel regressions. Start profiling on representative node (see profiling playbook).
4. If global and GPU_util is high -> capacity exhaustion: scale replicas or enable burst capacity.
5. If one model -> check recent deploys for that model, kernel flags, and quant profiles.
6. Temporary mitigations: route traffic to fallback model version or disable new kernel flag.
7. Post-incident: collect traces, open ticket linking to commit/rollout ID, and schedule a RCA.

Runbook B: GPU OOMs during steady-state
1. Identify node and process from alert. Capture nvml logs and /proc/<pid>/status.
2. Check model size and sequence length distribution; confirm if a single request caused the OOM (very long seq_len).
3. If OOM caused by cache growth: clear KV cache for model (admin API: POST /admin/model/<model>/cache/clear) and scale down allowed per-request max_seq_len.
4. If OOM due to memory leak: enable core dump and escalate to serving-runtime-engineering.

Runbook C: Degraded throughput with high kernel-launch overhead
1. Profile to confirm large number of small kernels (see profiling playbook).
2. Enable kernel coalescing flag for cluster: scheduler_policy.coalesce_small_kernels=true and monitor.
3. If coalescing introduces latency regressions, revert and open task to upstream kernel team.

Operational commands and quick snippets
- Check GPU utilization: nvidia-smi dmon -s u
- Dump host traces: sudo perf record -a -g -o perf.data -- sleep 60
- Restart model-executor gracefully: infractl runtime restart --service model-executor --rolling

7) Known issues (tracked)

ISSUE-2026-110: Intermittent p99 spikes on p4d with long-context models
- Symptoms: p99 increases by 2-5x under mixed workloads.
- Root cause (partial): contention in scheduler preemption code and high memcpy H2D after cache evictions.
- Mitigation: set scheduler_policy.latency_headroom_ms=50 and enable cache_proactive_prefetch=true.

ISSUE-2026-155: int8 kernel Kq produces rare numerical mismatch for redwood-large-v1
- Symptoms: token sampling divergence observed in canaries.
- Mitigation: temporarily disable Kq for redwood-large-v1 and run extended numeric tests.

ISSUE-2026-199: NVLINK topology regression causing degraded multi-GPU allreduce performance on new 8x A100 nodes
- Symptoms: higher-than-expected cross-GPU latency.
- Mitigation: pin clusters to previous kernel-driver combo while infra investigates.

8) Team wiki & knowledge base pointers
- Serving runtime team handbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-team-wiki-and-runbooks-2026.json
- Perf dashboard: internal link to perf-collector dashboard (add link in related_pages).
- Kernel dev notes & testing checklist: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-dev-checklist

9) Onboarding checklist for new runtime engineers
1. Read this document and serving-runtime-reference.
2. Run the standard benchmark suite locally against a dev image (tools/bench_runner.py with scenarios/dev.json).
3. Complete one profiling run end-to-end and submit artifacts.
4. Shadow oncall for two weeks.

Appendix A — Example scheduler YAML

scheduler_policy: |
  priority_windows_ms: [5, 20, 100]
  max_batch_size: 64
  latency_headroom_ms: 30
  preemption_enabled: true
  gpu_occupancy_target: 0.7
  coalesce_small_kernels: true

Appendix B — Example kernel micro-bench command

  python tools/kernel_bench.py --kernel K1 --seq_len 128 --batch 4 --repeat 500 --out /tmp/k1-seq128-b4.json

Appendix C — Minimal profiling artifact checklist (copy into ticket)
- nsight trace (.qdrep)
- torch.profiler (.json)
- bench_runner config (.json)
- machine metadata (nvidia-smi, driver, CUDA)
